title: Letter of Jeremiah

stories.title: 📜 Letter of Jeremiah
summaryBullets: Because of the sins that you have committed before God, you will be taken to Babylon as exiles by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians. (1:1).
Therefore when you have come to Babylon you will remain there for many years, for a long time, up to seven generations; after that I will bring you away from there in peace. (1:2).
Now in Babylon you will see gods made of silver and gold and wood that people carry on their shoulders and that cause the nations to fear. (1:3).
So beware of becoming at all like the foreigners or of letting fear of these gods possess you (1:4).
when you see the multitude before and behind them worshiping them. But say in your heart, “It is you, O Lord, whom we must worship.” (1:5).
For my angel is with you, and he is watching over your lives. (1:6).
Their tongues are smoothed by the carpenter, and they themselves are overlaid with gold and silver, but they are false and cannot speak. (1:7).
People take gold and make crowns for the heads of their gods, as they might for a young woman who loves ornaments. (1:8).
Sometimes the priests secretly take gold and silver from their gods and spend it on themselves (1:9).
or even give some of it to the prostitutes on the terrace. They deck their gods out with garments like humans—these gods of silver and gold and wood (1:10).
that cannot save themselves from rust and decay. When they have been dressed in purple robes, (1:11).
their faces are wiped because of the dust from the temple, which is thick upon them. (1:12).
One of them holds a scepter like a district judge but is unable to destroy anyone who offends it. (1:13).
Another has a dagger in its right hand and an ax but cannot defend itself from war and robbers. (1:14).
From this it is evident that they are not gods, so do not fear them. (1:15).
For just as someone’s dish is useless when it is broken, (1:16).

so are their gods when they have been set up in the temples. Their eyes are full of the dust raised by the feet of those who enter. And just as the gates are shut on every side against anyone who has offended a king, as though under sentence of death, so the priests make their temples secure with doors and locks and bars in order that they may not be plundered by robbers. (1:17).
They light more lamps for them than they light for themselves, though their gods can see none of them. (1:18).
They are just like a beam of the temple, but their hearts, it is said, are eaten away when crawling creatures from the earth devour them and their robes. They do not notice (1:19).
when their faces have been blackened by the smoke of the temple. (1:20).
Bats, swallows, and birds alight on their bodies and heads, and so do cats. (1:21).
From this you will know that they are not gods, so do not fear them. (1:22).
As for the gold that they wear for beauty, it will not shine unless someone wipes off the tarnish, for even when they were being cast, they did not feel it. (1:23).
They are bought without regard to cost, but there is no breath in them. (1:24).
Having no feet, they are carried on the shoulders of others, revealing to humans their worthlessness. And those who serve them are put to shame (1:25).

because, if any of these gods falls to the ground, they themselves must pick it up. If anyone sets it upright, it cannot move itself, and if it is tipped over, it cannot straighten itself. Gifts are placed before them just as before the dead. (1:26).
The priests sell the sacrifices that are offered to these gods and use the money themselves. Likewise their wives preserve some of the meat with salt but give none to the poor or helpless. (1:27).
Sacrifices to them may even be touched by women during their periods or after giving birth. Since you know by these things that they are not gods, do not fear them. (1:28).
For how can they be called gods? Women serve meals for gods of silver and gold and wood, (1:29).
and in their temples the priests sit with their clothes torn, their heads and beards shaved, and their heads uncovered. (1:30).
They howl and shout before their gods as some do at a funeral banquet. (1:31).
The priests take some of the clothing of their gods to clothe their wives and children. (1:32).
Whether one does evil to them or good, they will not be able to repay it. They cannot set up a king or depose one. (1:33).
Likewise, they are not able to give either wealth or money; if one makes a vow to them and does not keep it, they will not require it. (1:34).
They cannot save anyone from death or rescue the weak from the strong. (1:35).
They cannot restore sight to the blind; they cannot rescue one who is in distress. (1:36).
They cannot take pity on a widow or do good to an orphan. (1:37).
These things that are made of wood and overlaid with gold and silver are like stones from the mountain, and those who serve them will be put to shame. (1:38).

Why then must anyone think that they are gods or call them gods? Besides, even the Chaldeans themselves dishonor them, for when they see someone who cannot speak, they bring Bel and pray that the mute may speak, as though Bel were able to understand! (1:39).
Yet they themselves cannot perceive this and abandon them, for they have no sense. (1:40).
And the women, with cords around them, sit along the passageways, burning bran for incense. (1:41).
When one of them is led off by one of the passers-by and is taken to bed by him, she derides the woman next to her because she was not as attractive as herself and her cord was not broken. (1:42).
Whatever is done for these idols is false. Why then must anyone think that they are gods or call them gods? (1:43).
They are made by carpenters and goldsmiths; they can be nothing but what the artisans wish them to be. (1:44).
Those who make them will certainly not live very long themselves; (1:45).
how then can the things that are made by them be gods? They have left only lies and reproach for those who come after. (1:46).
For when war or calamity comes upon them, the priests consult together as to where they can hide themselves and their gods. (1:47).
How then can one fail to see that these are not gods, for they cannot save themselves from war or calamity? (1:48).
Since they are made of wood and overlaid with gold and silver, it will afterward be known that they are false. (1:49).
It will be manifest to all the nations and kings that they are not gods but the work of human hands and that there is no work of God in them. (1:50).
Who, then, does not know that they are not gods? (1:51).
For they cannot set up a king over a country or give rain to people. (1:52).
They cannot judge their own cause or deliver one who is wronged, for they have no power; (1:53).

they are like crows between heaven and earth. When fire breaks out in a temple of wooden gods overlaid with gold or silver, their priests will flee and escape, but the gods will be burned up like timbers. (1:54).
Besides, they can offer no resistance to king or enemy. Why then must anyone admit or think that they are gods? (1:55).
Gods made of wood and overlaid with silver and gold are unable to save themselves from thieves or robbers. (1:56).
Anyone who can will strip them of their gold and silver and of the robes they wear and go off with this plunder, and they will not be able to help themselves. (1:57).

So it is better to be a king who shows his courage or a household utensil that serves its owner’s need than to be these false gods, better even the door of a house that protects its contents than these false gods, better also a wooden pillar in a palace than these false gods. (1:58).
For sun and moon and stars are bright and, when sent to do a service, they are obedient. (1:59).
So also the lightning when it flashes is widely seen, and the wind likewise blows in every land. (1:60).
When God commands the clouds to go over the whole world, they carry out his command. (1:61).
And the fire sent from above to consume mountains and woods does what it is ordered. But these idols are not to be compared with them in appearance or power. (1:62).
Therefore one must not think that they are gods nor call them gods, for they are unable either to decide a case or to do good to anyone. (1:63).
Since you know, then, that they are not gods, do not fear them. (1:64).
They can neither curse nor bless kings; (1:65).
they cannot show signs in the heavens for the nations or shine like the sun or give light like the moon. (1:66).
The wild animals are better than they are, for they can flee to shelter and help themselves. (1:67).
So we have no evidence whatever that they are gods; therefore do not fear them. (1:68).
Like a scarecrow in a cucumber bed that guards nothing, so are their gods of wood, overlaid with gold and silver. (1:69).
In the same way, their gods of wood, overlaid with gold and silver, are like a thornbush in a garden on which every bird perches or like a corpse thrown out in the darkness. (1:70).
From the purple and linen that rot upon them you will know that they are not gods, and they will finally be consumed themselves and be a reproach in the land. (1:71).
Better, therefore, is someone upright who has no idols; such a person will be far above reproach. (1:72).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 29:1-7: Jeremiah's letter to the exiles carried off to Babylon.
Jeremiah 10:3-5: An idol cut from a tree and fastened with nails, like a scarecrow in a cucumber field.
Isaiah 44:9-20: The craftsman who burns half a log and worships an image made from the rest.
Isaiah 46:6-7: Gold weighed out to a goldsmith, and the image carried on the shoulder and set in place.
Psalm 115:4-8: Idols of silver and gold with mouths, eyes, ears, and hands that do nothing.

translationNotes.original: Greek: Ἐπιστολὴ Ἰερεμίου (Epistole Ieremiou, 'Letter of Jeremiah')
translationNotes.note: This text circulates under two addresses. Greek manuscripts carry it as a separate book with its own title; the Latin Vulgate attached it to the end of Baruch, so many Bibles print the same seventy-two verses as Baruch chapter 6 and cite them that way.

translationNotes.term: Overlaid with gold and carried on their shoulders
translationNotes.original: Greek: περικεχρυσωμένα (perikechrysomena, 'gilded around') and ἐπ' ὤμων (ep' omon, 'on shoulders')
translationNotes.note: Describes manufacture and festival practice. The image was carved from a wooden core, its features finished with a scraper by a carpenter, plated with hammered gold and silver leaf, then dressed in real purple cloth. At festivals it was lifted out of the temple on a litter borne by men, with crowds walking before and behind.

Temple staff lived off the image. Food offerings, lamps, and incense were the daily service, and a portion of what worshipers brought reverted to the priesthood as its income. The letter charges more than that: they strip silver and gold off the images, sell the offered meat for cash, and cut up the gods' wardrobe to clothe their own wives and children.

translationNotes.term: They are not gods, so do not fear them
translationNotes.original: Greek: οὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί· μὴ φοβηθῆτε αὐτούς (ouk eisin theoi; me phobethete autous)
translationNotes.note: A refrain, not a repetition error. The line returns at intervals to close each block of description, so the letter reads as a series of catalogues, each one ending in the same verdict. English editions print it as prose, which hides the structure.

stories.keyTakeaway: A letter to those going as exiles to Babylon, where they will see gods of silver, gold, and wood carried on shoulders. It catalogues how the images are made, robed, and paraded, and how the priests take their gold, offerings, and garments, repeating that these are not gods, so do not fear them.

intro:
The Letter of Jeremiah is a single chapter of seventy-two verses that a reader will meet under two names. In the Greek tradition it is a book of its own, titled Epistole Ieremiou (Ἐπιστολὴ Ἰερεμίου), the Letter of Jeremiah, and it stands at the end of the Jeremiah group after Lamentations. The Latin Vulgate attached it to the end of Baruch, so Bibles descended from the Latin print the same seventy-two verses as Baruch chapter 6 and cite them that way. The text is the same under either address; only its place in the table of contents changes. This edition follows the Greek and carries it as a separate book.

The letter presents itself as Jeremiah's, written to people about to be marched to Babylon. It opens, "Because of the sins that you have committed before God, you will be taken to Babylon as exiles by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians" (1:1), and tells them they will remain there many years, up to seven generations, after which God will bring them away in peace (1:2). Jeremiah, Yirmeyahu (יִרְמְיָהוּ) in Hebrew, a name built on the divine element for Yahuah, was the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests at Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin, and he prophesied from the thirteenth year of Josiah until the people of Jerusalem went into exile (Jeremiah 1:1-3). He did send a letter to the exiles in Babylon: Jeremiah 29:1-7 gives its text, carried by Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, telling the exiles to build houses, plant gardens, and seek the prosperity of the city they were carried to. Judah was taken apart in stages, with deportations under Nebuchadnezzar through 597 BC and the burning of the city in 587 BC, so the people addressed here had watched it happen and were about to be led into a capital full of gods they had never seen.

Those gods are the subject: "gods made of silver and gold and wood that people carry on their shoulders and that cause the nations to fear" (1:3). The letter is built as a run of catalogues, each closed by the same verdict. It describes manufacture: the carpenter smooths the tongue, gold and silver leaf goes over the wooden core, the figure is dressed in purple and crowned like a young woman who loves ornaments, and it cannot save itself from rust and decay (1:7-11). It describes the temple: dust thick on the faces, lamps lit for gods that see none of them, bats and swallows and cats settling on the heads (1:12-21). It describes the priests: they take gold and silver off the images and spend it, sell the offered meat, and cut up the gods' wardrobe to clothe their own wives and children (1:9-10, 27, 32). Then the refrain lands. "From this it is evident that they are not gods, so do not fear them" (1:15), and again in that form at 1:22, 1:28, 1:64, and 1:68; the same finding is restated, several times as a question, at 1:39, 1:43, 1:48, 1:50, 1:51, 1:55, 1:63, and 1:71. Thirteen times the argument halts and returns the same verdict. English editions set the letter as continuous prose, which hides that structure. It belongs to the same line of argument as Jeremiah 10:3-5, Isaiah 44:9-20, and Psalm 115:4-8, and it ends on the plainest comparisons it can reach for: better a household utensil, a door, a wooden pillar; the idols are a scarecrow in a cucumber bed that guards nothing (1:58, 1:69).

A Greek copy of the letter was in Judea before the turn of the era. The papyrus scrap catalogued as 7Q2, recovered from Qumran Cave 7 and assigned to the Hasmonean period, carries verses 43 and 44. The surviving text is Greek throughout. The old canon lists count the letter with the rest of the Jeremiah material rather than on its own: Origen's list, preserved in Eusebius, Church History 6.25, has "Jeremiah, with Lamentations and the epistle, in one"; Athanasius, Festal Letter 39 (AD 367), has "Jeremiah with Baruch, Lamentations and the Epistle, one book"; the Synod of Laodicea (c. AD 364) lists the same grouping. The Council of Trent (Fourth Session, 8 April 1546) named "Jeremias, with Baruch," which on the Vulgate arrangement takes in the letter as Baruch 6, and the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England (Article VI, 1563) list "Baruch the Prophet" on the same reckoning. The Eastern churches keep it where the Greek manuscripts put it, as a book by itself.
